headlines.label: Gross domestic income (real: GDP in krónur ÷ consumer prices)

indicators.label: Potential output (the central bank’s estimate from the labour market)

units.meaning: the percent difference from the no-change run’s level in the same month
the difference in percentage points of a rate or a share (a rate of 4% against 3% is +1 pp)
the percent difference from the no-change run’s level; positive is a stronger króna

the difference, in percentage points, of a ratio to nominal GDP: this month’s GDP at an annual rate, or GDP over the past 12 months, as the variable’s definition says. A ratio does not grow with the price level

expectations.theory: Interest-rate channel: a higher real rate lowers consumption and investment, so output falls with a lag of quarters.
expectations.source: Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (2005); CBI QMM v2.1 Monetary Bulletin rate experiment

expectations.theory: Slack, a stronger krona and lower asset prices reduce inflation after a lag.
expectations.source: Havranek and Rusnak (2013); CBI QMM v2.1

expectations.theory: Uncovered interest parity: a higher domestic rate attracts carry flows and strengthens the currency on impact.
expectations.source: Dornbusch (1976); CBI QMM v2.1 (0.67% per pp on impact)

expectations.theory: Okun’s law: lower output after tightening raises unemployment.
Asset-price channel: higher mortgage rates lower what buyers can pay for homes.
User cost of capital: a higher real loan rate lowers desired investment.
The mirror of tightening: a lower real rate stimulates demand and weakens the krona, raising inflation after a lag.
expectations.source: CBI QMM v2.1; Havranek and Rusnak (2013)

expectations.theory: Credit/bank-lending channel: dearer credit slows new borrowing, so the debt ratio falls over years.
expectations.source: Bernanke and Gertler (1995); Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1

expectations.theory: A higher real borrowing cost lowers investment, with a lag.
expectations.source: Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (2005), Journal of Political Economy 113

expectations.theory: Monetary tightening lowers output within two years.
expectations.source: Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (2005), Journal of Political Economy 113

expectations.theory: A key rate held above the neutral rate cools demand for years; tightening lowers output for more than a decade in the data. The model’s later reversal, through interest income with tax rates held, is at the strong end of the evidence and is not gated.
expectations.source: Jordà, Singh and Taylor (2024), The long-run effects of monetary policy, REStat; Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (2005); decision 0014

expectations.theory: A contractionary monetary stance lowers demand through the interest-rate channel.
expectations.source: Gali (2015), ch. 3 monetary policy shock; CBI QMM v2.1

expectations.theory: A tighter stance lowers inflation through slack and the exchange rate.
Moving the lever locks it: the key rate is held where it is set, above the neutral rate, for as long as it is set.
Uncovered interest parity: a wider rate gap strengthens the krona.
Okun’s law: tighter policy lowers output and raises unemployment in the medium run.
Asset-price channel: higher mortgage rates lower house prices.
An expansionary monetary stance raises demand in the medium run.
At the steady state the rule’s target equals the neutral rate. Handing the key rate back to the rule with no shock changes nothing (decisions 0004 and 0010: the same baseline, locked or not).
expectations.source: Decisions 0004 and 0010; Taylor (1993): the rule’s rate equals the neutral nominal rate at target inflation and zero gap

expectations.theory: With no shock, the rule’s suggestion equals the held neutral rate, so unlocking moves no policy instrument.
No shock means no policy reaction, so inflation stays at target, locked or not.
At the steady state debt is at its baseline ratio, so the debt rule’s shift is zero: handing income tax back to the rule with no shock changes nothing.
Locking with no shock freezes the key rate at the rate in force, the neutral rate, so nothing moves.
Locking income tax with no shock freezes it at the rate in force, the baseline rate, so nothing moves.
A sentiment (risk-premium) shock that raises the króna’s target weakens it at once and for most of a year, as in UIP with a risk-premium shock.
expectations.source: Dornbusch (1976); Central Bank of Iceland QMM risk-premium shock

expectations.theory: Exchange-rate pass-through: a weaker króna makes imports dearer in krónur and the CPI rises.
expectations.source: Campa and Goldberg (2005); Edwards and Cabezas (2021, Central Bank of Iceland)

expectations.theory: Pass-through works in reverse: a stronger króna lowers import prices and the CPI.
expectations.source: Campa and Goldberg (2005); Edwards and Cabezas (2021)

expectations.theory: Prices react before wages, so a depreciation squeezes real wages in the first year.
expectations.source: Blanchard, Macroeconomics (real-wage effect of depreciation); Central Bank of Iceland Monetary Bulletin

expectations.theory: Expenditure switching: a real depreciation makes Icelandic goods and tourism cheaper abroad.
Expenditure switching: dearer imports lower import volumes.
Once volumes have responded, the Marshall-Lerner condition makes the current account improve after a real depreciation (after any initial J-curve dip).
An inflation-targeting rule raises the key rate when depreciation-driven inflation rises.
Uncovered interest parity and the carry trade: a higher foreign rate makes króna assets less attractive, so the króna weakens.
UIP in reverse: lower foreign rates draw carry money into krónur and the króna strengthens.
The depreciation that follows a foreign rate rise passes through to import prices and the CPI.
The real depreciation switches foreign demand toward Icelandic goods (Mundell-Fleming).
The real depreciation makes imports dearer, so import volumes fall.
An inflation-targeting central bank tightens against imported inflation from the weaker króna.
An appreciation lowers inflation and the rule eases.
Higher foreign-currency prices pass through to import prices in krónur and to the CPI.
expectations.source: Campa and Goldberg (2005); Edwards and Cabezas (2021)

expectations.theory: Imported inflation: dearer imports raise 12-month CPI inflation.
Imported disinflation: cheaper imports lower CPI inflation.
Consumer prices rise before wages catch up, so real wages fall.
Fish and aluminium are priced in foreign currency, so higher world prices raise exporters’ króna revenue against mostly domestic costs.
expectations.source: Central Bank of Iceland Monetary Bulletin (export sectors); standard export-price income effect

expectations.theory: The inflation rule raises the key rate against imported inflation.
Purchasing-power parity: higher foreign prices lead, over years, to a stronger nominal króna.
PPP in reverse: lower foreign prices lead, over years, to a weaker nominal króna.
Export volumes rise with foreign demand (income elasticity of export demand).
expectations.source: Houthakker and Magee (1969), Review of Economics and Statistics

expectations.theory: Open-economy Keynesian multiplier: more export demand raises GDP before appreciation crowds it out.
expectations.source: Mundell (1963); Fleming (1962); Justiniano and Preston (2010), Journal of International Economics 81

expectations.theory: Okun’s law: higher output lowers unemployment.
Higher export earnings and a current-account surplus strengthen a floating currency (flow and portfolio-balance demand for krónur).
Exports rise faster than the imports they induce, so the current account improves.
expectations.source: BPM6 current-account identity; Obstfeld and Rogoff (1996)

expectations.theory: Dutch disease: a boom in one export sector appreciates the real exchange rate and crowds out other tradables such as tourism.
A fall in export demand lowers GDP through the multiplier.
A Taylor rule raises the policy rate when output rises above capacity.
Tourism is an export; losing it lowers GDP (Iceland 2020: tourism about −75%, GDP about −7%).
expectations.source: Hagstofa national accounts 2020; CBI Monetary Bulletin 2020/4

expectations.theory: Tourism is labour-intensive, so a collapse raises unemployment quickly.
Lost export earnings weaken a floating currency (the króna fell about 10% in trade-weighted terms in 2020).
Lower service exports worsen the current account.
A Taylor rule cuts the rate in a demand collapse (the CBI cut from 3% to 0.75% in 2020).
A tourism boom brings in foreign currency and appreciates the króna (as in 2013–17).
expectations.source: CBI Monetary Bulletin 2016–2017; Obstfeld and Rogoff (1996)

expectations.theory: Dutch disease: the appreciation from a tourism boom cuts króna revenue of exporters priced in foreign currency (fisheries’ margins fell in 2016–17).
More visitors raise output over the following quarters.
A collapse in visitors lowers output at once (2010, 2020).
A lasting export gain strengthens the currency in real and nominal terms (Dutch disease).

A collapse in export earnings weakens a floating currency, and pass-through lifts consumer prices for the first two years before slack pulls them down (2020: the króna fell nearly 10% in trade-weighted terms and inflation rose from 1.7% to 3.6% despite a 7% fall in GDP). The 2020 rise is an upper bound for tourism alone, since rate cuts, a housing boom and world prices also lifted it, so only the sign is tested.
expectations.source: CBI Monetary Bulletin 2020/4 and 2021/1; Landsbankinn, 8 January 2021; Edwards and Cabezas (2022), CBI Working Paper 85

expectations.theory: An inflation-targeting central bank brings inflation back to target after a lasting real shock, once it has learned the new neutral rate: the cycle of its learning dies out.
expectations.source: Svensson (1997), European Economic Review 41; Laubach and Williams (2003), Review of Economics and Statistics 85(4)

expectations.theory: A higher world price for a quota-bound export raises export earnings one for one on impact (a terms-of-trade gain).
With catches fixed by quotas, a price rise accrues to fisheries as resource rent.
expectations.source: Arnason (2008), on the Icelandic ITQ system

expectations.theory: Commodity currencies appreciate when the real price of their commodity exports rises.
expectations.source: Cashin, Céspedes and Sahay (2004), Journal of Development Economics

expectations.theory: Higher fisheries’ profits raise corporate tax (and the fishing fee).
expectations.source: Lög um veiðigjald nr. 145/2018; Hagstofa government finance

expectations.theory: A terms-of-trade gain raises real national income, through cheaper imports after appreciation and through owners’ income.
expectations.source: Kohli (2004), Review of Income and Wealth; Corden and Neary (1982)

expectations.theory: Dutch disease: a commodity boom appreciates the currency and shrinks other tradables.
A terms-of-trade loss on a quota-bound export lowers export earnings.
The spending effect of a domestically owned windfall: owners’ income, the fishing fee and cheaper imports after the appreciation raise household spending.
expectations.source: Corden and Neary (1982), Economic Journal 92; IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2012, ch. 4

expectations.theory: Dutch disease: the commodity windfall strengthens the currency in real terms, which crowds out the other exports (tourism and other goods and services).
expectations.source: Corden and Neary (1982), Economic Journal 92; Cashin, Céspedes and Sahay (2004)

expectations.theory: The terms-of-trade accounting effect: at the same volumes, a higher price for what Iceland sells buys more of what it consumes, so real gross domestic income rises (this one holds by construction; it is here as the accounting check beside the two behavioural ones).
expectations.source: Kohli (2004), Journal of International Economics 62; System of National Accounts 2008, ch. 15 (the trading gain)

expectations.theory: Quotas cap the catch, so a higher price goes mainly into fisheries’ profit (resource rent).
The state takes a share of resource rent through the fishing fee and corporate tax.
A lower price cuts fisheries’ profit, since volume is quota-bound.
A squeezed, indebted exporter invests less (cash-flow and leverage constraints on investment).
expectations.source: Fazzari, Hubbard and Petersen (1988), Brookings Papers 1988:1

expectations.theory: The smelters run at capacity and sell at the world price, so a price rise raises their profit.
Foreign-owned firms remit windfall profits to their parents as primary income paid abroad.
expectations.source: Eurostat bop_c6_a (Iceland inward FDI income); BPM6 ch. 11

expectations.theory: Exports rise by more than the extra income paid abroad, because taxes and domestic inputs stay in Iceland; the effect is small.
expectations.source: BPM6; CBI balance of payments commentary on aluminium

expectations.theory: Higher smelter profits raise corporate tax.
Capital-intensive smelters at capacity do not hire on a price change, and the windfall leaves the country, so jobs barely move.
expectations.source: Hagstofa THJ08420 (basic metals: small labour share); Eurostat bop_c6_a

expectations.theory: Foreign owners absorb the smelters’ losses when the aluminium price falls.
Lower export earnings, only partly offset by lower dividends abroad, worsen the current account a little.
Endogenous money: more mortgage lending raises the stock of household mortgage debt relative to GDP.
expectations.source: McLeay, Radia and Thomas (2014), Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin Q1

expectations.theory: Loans create deposits: extra bank lending expands broad money.
expectations.source: McLeay, Radia and Thomas (2014); Keen (2011) Debunking Economics

expectations.theory: A larger flow of mortgage credit bids up house prices.
expectations.source: Favara and Imbs (2015), American Economic Review; Keen’s credit accelerator

expectations.theory: Debt-financed demand: part of new borrowing and housing-wealth gains is spent.
expectations.source: Mian and Sufi (2011), American Economic Review; Biggs, Mayer and Pick (2010)

expectations.theory: A step up in the flow of net new credit is, by definition, a positive credit impulse on impact.
expectations.source: Biggs, Mayer and Pick (2010), ‘Credit and economic recovery’, DNB WP 218

expectations.theory: Credit-financed spending raises aggregate demand during the credit expansion.
expectations.source: Mian, Sufi and Verner (2017), Quarterly Journal of Economics

expectations.theory: Part of credit-financed demand leaks into imports, so the current account worsens during a credit boom.
Less mortgage credit flowing into housing lowers house prices.
expectations.source: Favara and Imbs (2015), American Economic Review

expectations.theory: A tighter debt-service-to-income cap limits new mortgage lending, so mortgage debt falls relative to baseline.
expectations.source: Kuttner and Shim (2016), Journal of Financial Stability

expectations.theory: Borrower-based limits reduce credit-financed housing demand and house-price growth.
expectations.source: Kuttner and Shim (2016); Alam et al. (2019), IMF WP/19/66

expectations.theory: Less bank lending means fewer deposits are created.
expectations.source: McLeay, Radia and Thomas (2014), Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin

expectations.theory: Less credit-financed spending and lower housing wealth reduce consumption.
expectations.source: Mian and Sufi (2011); Richter, Schularick and Shim (2019), Journal of International Economics

expectations.theory: A moderate tightening binds for the tail of borrowers near the limit (first-time buyers), so lending and debt fall modestly. This failed at the vetting, before the cap was made distributional.
expectations.source: Kuttner and Shim (2016); Central Bank of Iceland Financial Stability reports on DSTI rules

expectations.theory: A tight loan-to-value cap severely limits new purchase loans, so mortgage debt falls. This failed at the vetting, until the cap applied to gross lending.
expectations.source: Richter, Schularick and Shim (2019), Journal of International Economics; Cerutti, Claessens and Laeven (2017)

expectations.theory: Tighter LTV limits reduce house-price growth by constraining leveraged demand.
expectations.source: Kuttner and Shim (2016); Alam et al. (2019), IMF WP/19/66

expectations.theory: Less mortgage origination by banks creates fewer deposits.
expectations.source: McLeay, Radia and Thomas (2014), Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin

expectations.theory: Imposing a binding cap cuts the flow of net new credit on impact: a negative credit impulse.
expectations.source: Biggs, Mayer and Pick (2010), DNB WP 218

expectations.theory: Less credit-financed spending and lower housing wealth reduce consumption after a sharp LTV tightening.
expectations.source: Richter, Schularick and Shim (2019), Journal of International Economics

expectations.theory: Portfolio balance: pension funds sell krónur to buy foreign assets, so the króna weakens.
expectations.source: Kouri (1976); Branson (1977); CBI and pension funds’ March 2020 pause of FX purchases to support the króna

expectations.theory: Repatriation means buying krónur, so the króna strengthens.
Exchange-rate pass-through: a weaker króna raises import and consumer prices.
expectations.source: Central Bank of Iceland QMM documentation; Campa and Goldberg (2005), Review of Economics and Statistics

expectations.theory: Balance-of-payments identity: a private financial outflow is matched by a current-account surplus, through expenditure switching.
expectations.source: Godley and Lavoie (2007), Monetary Economics, ch. 12

expectations.theory: A weaker real króna makes exports more competitive.
A weaker real króna makes imports dearer, so volumes fall.
Raising the target foreign share raises the actual foreign share as the funds rebalance.
An inflation-targeting central bank raises its rate against depreciation-driven inflation.
expectations.source: Taylor (1993); Central Bank of Iceland inflation-targeting framework

expectations.theory: A nominal settlement raises the real wage on impact because prices are set as a markup on smoothed costs and catch up only with a lag (battle of markups).
expectations.source: Blanchard (1986), ‘The wage price spiral’, QJE; CBI Monetary Bulletin 2026/2 Box 2, ‘Wages +10%’

expectations.theory: Profit squeeze: labour costs rise before prices, so margins compress first; profits are a residual and fall more than proportionally.
expectations.source: Goodwin (1967); first-round arithmetic on Hagstofa THJ08420 (2025) used in calibration.ts SRC.squeeze

expectations.theory: Exporters are price-takers in world markets (main-course model), so higher wages cut their margins directly.
expectations.source: Aukrust (1977), the Norwegian main-course model; Carlin & Soskice (2015), Macroeconomics, ch. 11

expectations.theory: Cost pass-through: higher unit labour costs raise domestic prices and CPI inflation within quarters.
expectations.source: CBI Monetary Bulletin 2026/2 Box 2; Bobeica, Ciccarelli & Vansteenkiste (2019), ECB WP 2235

expectations.theory: Pass-through works both ways: a nominal wage cut lowers unit costs and, over time, the price level.
expectations.source: Daníelsson (2021), CBI research on CPI and unit labour costs moving together; Blanchard (1986)

expectations.theory: Labour demand falls when the real product wage rises; the labour market then does part of the work of restoring the wage share.
expectations.source: CBI DYNIMO results in MB 2026/2; Lichter, Peichl & Siegloch (2015), European Economic Review, meta-analysis of labour-demand elasticities

expectations.theory: An inflation-targeting central bank raises the policy rate in response to higher inflation and expectations (Taylor rule).
expectations.source: Taylor (1993); CBI MB 2026/2 ‘Wages +10%’: policy rate +1 to +1.5 pp at the peak

expectations.theory: Higher domestic costs appreciate the real exchange rate and erode export competitiveness.
expectations.source: Aukrust (1977); Carlin & Soskice (2015), open-economy wage-setting/price-setting model

expectations.theory: A general pay rise is passed on to prices (battle of markups).
expectations.source: Blanchard (1986), Journal of Political Economy 94; CBI Monetary Bulletin 2026/2, Box 2

expectations.theory: Nominal pay is set for the contract; prices catch up only gradually.
expectations.source: Bårdsen et al. (2005), The Econometrics of Macroeconomic Modelling

expectations.theory: Plain runs (no companion). The buffer acts only on job changes from baseline; with no shock there is nothing to buffer and nothing should move.
On top of a 20% fall in foreign demand: when more of a job loss is met by workers leaving, unemployment rises less (migration as regional/national labour-market adjustment).
expectations.source: Blanchard & Katz (1992), BPEA; IMF (2026) Iceland Article IV on the flattened Beveridge curve

expectations.theory: On top of a 20% fall in foreign demand: with no migration response, every lost job adds to unemployment, so unemployment rises more than with the baseline buffer.
expectations.source: Blanchard & Katz (1992); Jauer, Liebig, Martin & Puhani (2019), Regional Studies

expectations.theory: On top of a 20% fall in foreign demand: a smaller rise in unemployment means less slack in the wage Phillips curve, so real wages fall less.
expectations.source: Phillips (1958) and Blanchard & Katz (1999) wage curves; IMF (2026) Iceland Article IV

expectations.theory: On top of a 20% fall in foreign demand: without a migration buffer the whole job loss becomes slack, so wage moderation is stronger.
expectations.source: Blanchard & Katz (1999), AER P&P, wage curves

expectations.theory: On top of a 20% fall in foreign demand: fewer residents are unemployed, so fewer benefits are paid (a smaller automatic-stabiliser outflow).
On top of a 20% fall in foreign demand: more emigration in a bust removes housing demand, so real house prices fall more. This failed at the vetting (LAB-4), before migrants carried housing demand.
expectations.source: Saiz (2007), Journal of Urban Economics; CBI Financial Stability reports on population growth and housing demand

expectations.theory: A labour-supply shock raises unemployment until the newcomers are absorbed.
More job-seekers slow wage growth (the wage Phillips curve).

A lasting rise in the labour force raises output for good: newcomers work, earn and spend (a 2% larger labour force, about 1–2% more output). This failed at the re-vetting, while the newcomers left again (NETIMM-VANISHES).
expectations.source: Borjas (1995), Journal of Economic Perspectives 9(2); Ottaviano and Peri (2012), Journal of the European Economic Association 10(1); CBI Monetary Bulletin 2018 on immigration in 2017–19

expectations.theory: Newcomers who stay find jobs as demand grows with them, so employment ends higher.
expectations.source: Ottaviano and Peri (2012), Journal of the European Economic Association 10(1)

expectations.theory: More residents need homes, so a lasting rise in population raises house prices while supply adjusts.
A higher replacement rate lengthens job search and raises reservation wages, so equilibrium unemployment rises.
expectations.source: Layard, Nickell and Jackman (1991), Unemployment; Mortensen and Pissarides (1994)

expectations.theory: A higher replacement rate lengthens job search and raises reservation wages, so equilibrium unemployment rises.
expectations.source: Layard, Nickell and Jackman (1991), Unemployment; Mortensen and Pissarides (1994)

expectations.theory: Less generous benefits shorten job search, so equilibrium unemployment falls.
expectations.source: Layard, Nickell and Jackman (1991), Unemployment; Mortensen and Pissarides (1994)

expectations.theory: A higher reservation wage raises the rate of unemployment at which inflation is steady, and an inflation-targeting central bank does not hold unemployment below it, so fewer people work. (With both policy levers locked, the key rate held, the benefits’ support to demand outweighs this: lever-vetting open item on benefits.)
expectations.source: Layard, Nickell and Jackman (1991), Unemployment; Mortensen and Pissarides (1994), Review of Economic Studies

expectations.theory: Fewer people in work produce less once policy has leaned against the higher normal unemployment.
Tax multiplier: a higher income-tax rate cuts disposable income and consumption, and output follows through the multiplier.
expectations.source: Romer and Romer (2010, AER); Mertens and Ravn (2013, AER); IMF WEO Oct 2010 ch. 3

expectations.theory: Tax multiplier, symmetric: a tax cut raises disposable income, consumption and output.
expectations.source: Romer and Romer (2010, AER); Guajardo, Leigh and Pescatori (2014, JEEA)

expectations.theory: Consumption function: spending falls with after-tax income, gradually because of habit.
expectations.source: Parker, Souleles, Johnson and McClelland (2013, AER); Cloyne (2013, AER)

expectations.theory: Arithmetic: disposable income is gross income minus tax.
Budget arithmetic: automatic stabilisers win back only part of a tax rise (budget semi-elasticity about 0.4–0.5).
expectations.source: Price, Dang and Botev (2015), OECD Economics Department WP 1275

expectations.theory: Government budget constraint: surpluses repay debt.
expectations.source: Bohn (1998, QJE); Godley and Lavoie (2007) ch. 3

expectations.theory: Sectoral balances and twin deficits: fiscal tightening lowers import demand and improves the current account.
expectations.source: Godley (1999, Levy Institute); Abbas, Bouhga-Hagbe, Fatás, Mauro and Velloso (2011, IMF Economic Review)

expectations.theory: A locked POLICY lever never moves unless the user moves it. The Taylor rule only suggests.
With the key rate locked, the central bank’s rule only suggests, whatever the budget does.

With the key rate held and tax rates fixed there is no nominal anchor (decision 0014): a lasting tax rise leaves the held rate too high for the new economy, so demand stays weak and output below baseline for as long as it is held (Wicksell’s cumulative process). Only the sign is gated; the model’s long run has no level to test against.
expectations.source: Wicksell (1898), Interest and Prices; Godley and Lavoie (2007), Levy WP 494; decision 0014

expectations.theory: A higher income tax cuts disposable income and so spending (with a cash buffer, gradually).
expectations.source: Godley and Lavoie (2007), Monetary Economics, ch. 3

expectations.theory: Tax multiplier, damped by the central bank easing in response.
expectations.source: IMF WEO Oct 2010 ch. 3; Batini, Eyraud, Forni and Weber (2014, IMF TNM/14/04)

expectations.theory: Tax multiplier, symmetric, damped by monetary tightening.
Taylor rule: fiscal tightening lowers inflation and the output gap, so the rule cuts the key rate.
Taylor rule leans against a fiscal stimulus.
Budget arithmetic: a higher tax rate raises revenue, and stabilisers only partly offset it.
expectations.source: Price, Dang and Botev (2015), OECD WP 1275

expectations.theory: Government budget constraint: surpluses reduce debt.
Arithmetic: higher tax means lower disposable income.
VAT pass-through: a higher consumption tax raises consumer prices, almost fully for standard-rate changes; a lasting rise moves the price level once.
expectations.source: Benedek, De Mooij, Keen and Wingender (2020), International Tax and Public Finance 27

expectations.theory: VAT pass-through of a cut, which may be slower than for a rise.
expectations.source: Benedek et al. (2020); Benzarti, Carloni, Harju and Kosonen (2020, JPE)

expectations.theory: Incidence: a broad consumption tax lowers the real consumer wage (W ÷ CPI). Its burden falls on real factor incomes.
expectations.source: Atkinson and Stiglitz (1980), Lectures on Public Economics ch. 6; Fullerton and Metcalf (2002), Handbook of Public Economics

expectations.theory: Higher consumer prices cut real purchasing power and real consumption.
expectations.source: Crossley, Low and Wakefield (2009, Fiscal Studies), UK VAT cut; Cashin and Unayama (2016, REStat), Japan

expectations.theory: Budget arithmetic: more VAT revenue, only partly offset by a smaller base. From m6 so the one-off indexation accrual has passed.
CPI indexation: most Icelandic mortgages are indexed, so a price-level rise adds to their principal.
expectations.source: Central Bank of Iceland, Financial Stability (2024); Act 38/2001 on interest and indexation

expectations.theory: A locked POLICY lever never moves unless the user moves it.
VAT pass-through raises consumer prices at once, and with the key rate held the level stays above baseline for the first years while slack pulls inflation down only gradually.
expectations.source: Benedek, De Mooij, Keen and Wingender (2020), International Tax and Public Finance; decision 0014

expectations.theory: A tax increase lowers real disposable income and demand (tax multiplier).
expectations.source: IMF WEO Oct 2010 ch. 3; Coenen et al. (2012, AEJ: Macro)

expectations.theory: Government purchases add directly to demand and output (Keynesian multiplier).
expectations.source: Blanchard and Perotti (2002, QJE); Ramey (2019, JEP)

expectations.theory: Cutting government purchases lowers demand and output.
expectations.source: Blanchard and Perotti (2002); Guajardo, Leigh and Pescatori (2014, JEEA)

expectations.theory: More public staff and higher output raise employment (Okun’s law).
Higher spending worsens the budget balance, only partly offset by extra tax revenue.
expectations.source: Government budget identity; Girouard and André (2005, OECD WP 434)

expectations.theory: Import leakage: part of public purchases and of the extra income is spent on imports.
expectations.source: Batini et al. (2014, IMF TNM); Statistics Iceland (imports about 43% of GDP)

expectations.theory: An inflation-targeting central bank leans against a demand expansion (Taylor rule).
Persistent deficits accumulate into debt (government budget constraint).
With the policy rate held, a tighter labour market raises wage and price inflation (Phillips curve).
Government purchases add directly to demand and output.
Cutting government purchases lowers demand and output.
Labour-intensive public services hire staff directly; higher output raises jobs (Okun’s law).
Higher spending worsens the budget balance.
The Taylor rule leans against a demand expansion.
With the policy rate held, a tighter labour market raises inflation (Phillips curve).
Government purchases add directly to demand and output.
Cutting government purchases lowers demand and output.
Higher public spending raises employment (Okun’s law).
Higher spending worsens the budget balance.
Import leakage from purchases and from the extra income.
The Taylor rule leans against a demand expansion.
Public investment raises demand; its domestic content raises output at once.
expectations.source: IMF WEO Oct 2014, ch. 3 (Abiad et al. 2016)

expectations.theory: Cutting public investment lowers demand and output.
Public investment is part of gross fixed capital formation.
Investment goods have high import content in a small open economy.
Sectoral balances: a larger public deficit with extra imports worsens the current account (twin deficits).
expectations.source: Godley and Lavoie (2007); Abbas et al. (2011, IMF Econ Review)

expectations.theory: Higher spending worsens the budget balance.
The Taylor rule leans against a demand expansion.
Construction output raises employment with a lag (Okun’s law).
Transfers raise recipients’ disposable income, and they spend part of it (MPC).
expectations.source: Parker, Souleles, Johnson and McClelland (2013, AER); Wilcox (1989, JPE)

expectations.theory: Cutting transfers lowers recipients’ income and spending.
A transfer is household income: disposable income rises by the after-tax amount.
The transfer multiplier: extra spending by recipients raises output, by less than purchases do.
Higher transfers worsen the budget balance.
Persistent deficits accumulate into debt.
The Taylor rule leans against the rise in demand.
Benefits to young families (high MPC, often liquidity-constrained) raise their spending.

levers.label: Key interest rate
levers.description: The central bank’s key interest rate. Unlocked (the default), the central bank’s inflation rule sets it and the lever follows the rule. Move the lever, or close its padlock, to hold the rate yourself; the rule then only suggests a rate beside the lever.
levers.definition: Level of the key rate in percent a year. Unlocked (the default) the central bank’s inflation rule sets it every month, and the lever shows the rule’s rate. Moving the lever, or closing its padlock, locks it: the key rate is then held at the lever’s level from the month it is set until you move it again, and the rule only suggests a rate beside the lever. Closing the padlock holds the rate in force that month. Unlocking hands the key rate back to the rule, which moves from the rate you held about a tenth of the way toward where it is heading each month, so the rate does not jump. The default, 3%, is the neutral rate, so the baseline is unchanged. While the key rate is locked, nothing anchors inflation but people’s partial trust in the target: a lasting change that keeps unemployment off its normal rate keeps inflation off target for as long as you hold the rate, and the price level drifts (Wicksell’s cumulative process; decisions 0002 §6 and 0014). Held while income tax is unlocked, the debt rule pays for the higher interest bill with higher taxes, so a higher rate keeps cooling the economy: at 6%, output is about 1.4% below baseline after a year and about 2.5% below from the fourth year until about the tenth, still 1.1% below after 20 years, with the price level 11% lower, government debt 27 points of GDP higher and income tax 3.1 points higher. (The debt rule stands aside while the central bank’s own rule is heading below zero, and that rule now reads slack from unemployment, decision 0012, so taxes rise sooner than they did: with the fixed potential output was 0.8% below after 20 years.) At 15% the interest bill runs away: debt ends about 245 points of GDP higher and income tax 35 points higher, rates no government could sustain; treat that run as showing why real central banks do not hold such rates, not as a forecast. Held at 0%, output is 1.4% higher after a year and 3.4% after 20, with the price level 19% higher and still rising. With income tax locked too, nothing in the model reacts, and any lasting move reverses its effect on output after about ten years, roughly in proportion to its size. That is the interest-income channel of stock-flow models (Godley and Lavoie’s model PC; decision 0014). A rise first cools the economy, but the government then pays more interest every year, as its bonds are refinanced at the higher rate (about a fifth of them a year) and on a debt that grows with that interest, and with tax rates held that interest is private income. It reaches people two ways: at once, as interest on older households’ bonds and deposits, which they spend; and slowly, through the pension funds, whose extra income is credited to members’ pension rights and raises pensions only as the rights are paid out (at 6%, pensions buy about 0.7% more after a year, 5% more after five years and 13% more after 20). Once enough debt has built up, spending out of that income outweighs the higher rate. That is the strong end of the evidence: tightening does lower output for more than a decade (Jordà, Singh and Taylor 2024), but savers who gain interest income spend little of it (Auclert 2019), so a real economy would reverse later, if at all. At 4%, output is about 0.5% below baseline after a year and about 0.8% below at the trough early in the fourth year, back above it from about month 138 and about 0.7% above after 20 years; bigger moves reverse sooner and much further. At 6%, output is 2.3% lower at the trough, above baseline from month 126 and 2.9% higher after 20 years, with inflation 0.9 point higher. At the top of the range the run becomes explosive: at 15%, output falls 10% by the fourth year, is above baseline from month 110, and after 20 years is 34% higher with unemployment 3 points lower, the price level 61% higher, real wages 38% lower, government debt 320 points of GDP higher and the deficit 42% of GDP, still accelerating. It explodes because interest compounds on a debt that fixed tax rates never pay down, with the interest rate far above the economy’s growth, not because the central bank prints money to pay the bills: the model has no route by which it would, and no risk premium on government debt. In real economies a debt this large would also raise questions of fiscal dominance, which the model leaves out. Nor does the model follow the fiscal theory of the price level, the leading theory for a held rate with fixed taxes, which predicts a one-time jump in prices after which inflation settles: here prices keep trending. A cut mirrors this.

levers.label: Bank lending appetite
levers.description: Extra (or less) mortgage lending banks are willing to push each year.
levers.definition: Level shift in households’ desired new mortgage borrowing, % of baseline GDP a year, split between the young and working age by their share of mortgage debt; persistent while set and still subject to the debt-service and loan-to-value caps. A lasting push has a lasting effect: at −3, output is about 1.1% lower after five years and still about 0.16% lower after twenty with the policy rules acting, where the central bank eases but learns its neutral rate only slowly; with both policy levers locked the fall is deeper at first (1.7% after five years) and then turns into a small rise. A push up with the policy rules acting leaves the real króna slightly weaker for the first three years (+3: about 0.1% on average over months 12–36), where an inflation-targeting central bank that tightens should make it stronger: the rule reads the boom from jobs, which lag output, so it tightens late and little, and the krónur the boom’s import bill leaves with non-residents outweigh the pull of the higher rate (a known gap, lever-vetting open item 4, decision 0013). Setting it back to 0 ends the push; loans already made are repaid over their term.

levers.label: Foreign demand
levers.description: Demand abroad for Icelandic goods and services other than tourism and aluminium: it moves other exporters one for one and fisheries lightly.
levers.definition: Level shift in foreign demand, in percent of baseline, persistent while set. It reaches export volumes over a few quarters (about a fifth in the first month, 95% within a year): other exporters’ volume moves by the full percentage and marine volume by 0.3 of it (catches are capped by quotas). Tourism has its own lever and the smelters run at capacity. Held for many years, a lasting change in exports also changes the króna for good: non-residents’ krónur keep draining (or piling up) until the current account closes, so a rise ends in a stronger real króna that takes back other exports, and a fall in a weaker one (decision 0002 §6). With the policy rules acting output and unemployment end near baseline (at +20 unemployment about 0.1 point higher after 20 years). With the key rate held (both policy levers locked) the króna keeps strengthening and prices keep falling after a rise, so after about ten years output ends below baseline and unemployment above it (+20: output 0.8% lower and unemployment 0.3 point higher after 20 years), and the reverse after a fall: a known gap in how the current account closes, not a lasting cost of exporting more. Setting it back to 0 returns demand to baseline the same way.

levers.label: Tourism
levers.description: Foreign visitors’ spending: it drives the tourism sector.
levers.definition: Level shift in tourism export volume (what foreign visitors buy), in percent of baseline, persistent while set. A rise reaches visitor numbers over a few quarters (95% within a year), limited by flights, hotel rooms and staff; a fall hits within a month or so, as in 2010 and 2020. Tourism firms’ revenue, jobs and imports follow. Held for many years, a lasting change in exports also changes the króna for good: non-residents’ krónur keep draining (or piling up) until the current account closes, so a rise ends in a stronger real króna that takes back other exports, and a fall in a weaker one (decision 0002 §6). With the policy rules acting output and unemployment end near baseline (at +30 unemployment about 0.1 point higher after 20 years). A very large fall is different: at −60, about the 2020 collapse, the central bank cuts gradually, because it reads slack from unemployment, which rises more slowly than output falls, while the weaker króna lifts inflation at first: foreign currency is about 12% dearer after a year (the 2020 slump took about 10% off the trade-weighted króna), inflation is higher for the first two years, and the key rate is still about 1.5% after a year and reaches zero in the fourth year, where it stays. Prices then fall (8% lower after 20 years, inflation still about 0.1 point below target), and output is still about 1.2% lower and unemployment 0.5 point higher after twenty years. Until the key rate is stuck at zero the debt rule leans against the rising debt, and income tax ends 1.3 points higher; from then on it raises no taxes (its escape clause), and without that clause it raised income tax by over 3 points and output ended almost 4% lower. (While the central bank measured slack against a fixed capacity it cut to zero within about half a year, and output ended about 1% lower with no tax rise; decision 0012.) With the key rate held (both policy levers locked) the króna keeps strengthening and prices keep falling after a rise, so after about ten years output ends below baseline and unemployment above it (+30: output 1.2% lower and unemployment 0.47 point higher; +10: 0.4% and 0.16 point after 20 years), and the reverse after a fall: a known gap in how the current account closes, not a lasting cost of exporting more. Setting it back to 0 ends it the same way.

levers.label: Króna sentiment shock
levers.description: A one-off shift in what investors think the króna is worth. Negative means a weaker króna.
levers.definition: One-off shift in the króna’s target value by this percentage (−10: a target 10% weaker), fired once. The króna falls by most of it within a quarter (−10: about 9% by month 3). At first the current account worsens: imports are invoiced in foreign currency, so the import bill in krónur rises at once, while volumes take months to respond (a J-curve). Then portfolio balance pulls the króna back, more slowly than the krónur non-residents hold alone would, because the market also prices the krónur still flowing to them. Pension funds sell some of their foreign assets, now worth more in krónur, to get back to their target share (about 1.5–2% of GDP a year at first), and once trade has turned, the surplus the weaker króna brings drains krónur too. With fewer krónur to hold, non-residents accept a stronger króna. With the policy rules acting the central bank also raises the key rate, and the wider rate gap adds to the pull; with both policy levers locked the key rate does not move. Part of the fall is gone after a year: about a quarter with the policy rules acting and a fifth with both policy levers locked (−10: about 7% weaker at month 12 with the policy rules acting, 8% with both policy levers locked); about half after two years with the policy rules acting and two-fifths with both policy levers locked. In real terms half of the fall is gone about a year after its low with the policy rules acting and a year and a half with both policy levers locked: faster than the two to three years the Central Bank of Iceland’s model implies (a known gap, decision 0013). The shift in the target itself fades at only about 10% of its size a year, so the króna recovers well before it has faded. No one here owes foreign currency (pension funds and the central bank hold foreign assets), so a weaker króna raises residents’ net worth; the squeeze comes from dearer imports cutting real wages and from CPI indexation of mortgages and government debt. Before 2008, firms’ and households’ foreign-currency loans made a fall in the króna far more damaging (Krugman 1999; Céspedes, Chang and Velasco 2004). Prices, rates and trade respond.

levers.label: Foreign interest rate
levers.description: Interest rates abroad; a higher rate pulls carry money and pension savings out of krónur, so the króna weakens.
levers.definition: Level shift in the foreign interest rate, in percentage points, applied at once and persistent while set. The rate gap with abroad narrows, so carry traders sell króna bonds and pension funds raise their foreign target by 1 point of assets per point: the króna weakens for about the first six years (about 1.2% on average over the first two per point with the policy rules acting). It also raises the yield on the central bank’s reserves and on the funds’ foreign bonds (not their shares). The central bank first keeps the extra in its reserves, in foreign currency, then slowly sells what is above its reserve target back into krónur, so its reserves settle a little above target (about 0.6 of a point of GDP per point held); the funds’ extra income is paid home in krónur. Spent at home, that income slowly strengthens the króna: per point held with the policy rules acting the króna is back near its start after about six years and about 1.6% stronger after twenty, with prices about where they started and inflation slightly below target (with both policy levers locked about 4% stronger and prices about 2% lower after twenty, and more than proportionally so for large rises). That drift is a known gap (decision 0002 §6): the model has no foreign-currency debt that pays the foreign rate, so Iceland’s income from abroad rises by about 0.3% of GDP a year per point, where its roughly matched foreign-currency assets and debts would make it much less. Setting it back to 0 ends it.

levers.label: World fish prices
levers.description: What foreign buyers pay for Icelandic fish, in foreign currency.
levers.definition: Level shift in the world price of marine products, in percent, on top of the world-prices lever; applied at once and persistent while set. Quotas cap the catch, so most of the change goes into fisheries’ revenue and profit; volume moves only a little (about 3% at +30), through fuller use of quotas, the product mix and aquaculture, and the stronger króna that follows takes back part of the gain. A third of any change in fisheries’ profit goes to or comes back from the state as the fishing fee two years later, so a fall in prices lowers the fee as a rise raises it. Fisheries normally pay out only about 4% of their profit, so their payout sits close to zero: a small fall in their profit, or even an unrelated shock that raises their debt a little, stops dividends or has owners putting money in for years, which makes their responses lopsided (a known gap: recalibrating the baseline payout needs a new steady-state target, decision 0003). The spending comes first and the stronger króna follows, and in the first year the two about cancel in output (+30: 0.05% lower over the first year, where the windfall’s spending lifts household consumption about 1.5% over three years and tourism and other exports fall about 4% over years 1–5; decision 0013). Held for many years, a rise keeps strengthening the króna, which takes back other exports: at +30 output is about 0.4% higher but unemployment 0.2 point higher after 20 years with the policy rules acting, and output 2.7% lower and unemployment 1.1 points higher with the key rate held (both policy levers locked), a known gap in how the current account closes (decision 0002 §6). Setting it back to 0 ends it.

levers.label: Wage settlement
levers.description: A one-off jump in nominal wage rates, as after a collective agreement.
levers.definition: One-off level shift: the wage rate, private and public, jumps by this percentage in the month the lever is fired. It is not reversed; afterwards wages follow the Phillips curve. Firms price the pay rise in within a few months, so at first the real-wage gain erodes mainly through prices (+10% with both policy levers locked: consumer prices about 2.6% higher after a year, wages about 2 points below their new level). Wage bargainers then work the rest off over the following rounds (the error correction, with a lag of about a year), until wages are back in line with what firms earn per unit of value added. With labour about half of unit cost, domestic prices rise by only about two-thirds of the wage rise at a given exchange rate, so in the end wages give back most of the settlement: with the policy rules acting the price level is about 3.1% higher after six years and about 2.8% after twenty, with wages a little above it. That is below the Central Bank of Iceland’s figure of about 4%: the model gives wages back too fast in the first year, a known gap (decisions 0011 and 0012). levers.label: Net immigration
levers.description: A wave of workers arriving from abroad (or leaving), looking for work.
levers.definition: One-off shift in the labour force, in thousands of people of working age, in the month the lever is fired (5 thousand is about 2% of the labour force). They stay. They arrive looking for work, so unemployment rises at once, mostly among the young and working age; wage growth slows through the Phillips curve, their benefits add to spending and they need homes. They take the first new jobs as demand grows with them, and while jobs are short a part of the shortfall moves on again (the migration buffer). At 5 thousand, unemployment is about 1.4 points higher at first. With the policy rules acting, where the central bank counts them in the economy’s capacity and eases, unemployment is 0.2 point higher after 20 years, with jobs 1.7%, output 3.2% and real house prices 5.8% higher; with both policy levers locked unemployment stays about 0.8 point higher, and jobs end 0.9%, output 1.2% and house prices 1.2% higher. A negative value is emigration, with the reverse effects. To size the share of job changes met by migration, use the migration buffer.

levers.label: Income-tax rate
levers.description: Changes the average tax rate on wages, benefits and pensions. Unlocked (the default), the debt rule sets the rate and the lever follows it. Move the lever, or close its padlock, to hold the rate yourself; the debt rule then only suggests a value beside the lever.
levers.definition: Level shift in the income-tax rate, in percentage points from its baseline. Unlocked (the default) the debt rule sets the shift every month, leaning against government debt, and the lever shows it. Moving the lever, or closing its padlock, locks it: the shift is then the lever’s, applied in the month it is set and held until you move it again, and the debt rule only suggests a value beside the lever. Setting it back to 0 while locked returns the rate to its baseline. Unlocking hands the rate back to the debt rule, which moves from the rate you held about 4% of the way toward where it is heading each month. Held while the key rate is unlocked, the central bank leans against the tax change, but nothing pays a tax cut back or spends the surplus of a rise, and the interest on a growing debt is income that is spent, so the central bank cannot steady the economy on its own (with no fiscal rule and an active monetary rule there is no stable path, Leeper 1991): at −2.5 points, output is about 0.5% higher after a year and 3.2% after 20, with government debt 47 points of GDP higher and the key rate 4.8 points higher, all still rising; at +2.5 the mirror, the key rate at zero from about the fifteenth year and output 3.3% lower after 20 years, still falling, with the price level 10.9% lower and the króna 16% stronger. At ±10 these paths run away within 20 years. To lean on the debt rule without holding the rate, lock the lever, set it, and unlock it again: the rule carries on from your rate. With the key rate held (locked), a lasting change that keeps unemployment off its normal rate keeps inflation off target: after a lasting tax rise, say, the held rate is too high for the new economy, so prices keep falling while unemployment stays up (Wicksell’s cumulative process). With the key rate held and tax rates fixed, nothing but people’s partial trust in the target anchors prices: expectations are only half anchored to it, so the long-run Phillips curve is not vertical (decisions 0002 §6 and 0014), and the króna follows domestic prices. Output and unemployment keep drifting too, for decades; whether they would ever settle is an open question about the model, not a law of economics (decision 0014). After 20 years with both policy levers locked, income tax +2.5 points leaves output about 3.9% lower (0.6% after a year, 2.1% after five) and unemployment 1.2 points higher, both still moving, with the price level 15% lower and the króna 22% stronger; VAT +2.5 points leaves output 2.1% lower and the price level 6.7% lower, so with the key rate held a VAT rise ends up lowering prices; health spending −3% of GDP leaves output 6% lower and unemployment 3.4 points higher; public investment −3% leaves output 9% lower. Treat such effects beyond a few years as a picture of an economy without its nominal anchor. With the policy levers unlocked, the central bank’s rule, which reads slack from unemployment and slowly learns its neutral rate, brings inflation back: after 20 years within about 0.1 point for VAT and 0.05 for transfers, but benefits +30 points leave unemployment about 1 point higher, and public spending ±3% of GDP leaves inflation up to about 0.3 point (a rise) or 0.7 point (a cut) off target and unemployment 0.2–1.3 points off normal, because public services move jobs more than output and the rule’s estimate of the neutral rate reaches its limit (the lever report shows the rate the economy would need, the implied neutral rate, with the debt rule still reacting to it).

levers.label: VAT rate
levers.description: Changes the effective VAT rate on consumer spending; shops pass it into prices over a few months.
levers.definition: Level shift in the effective VAT rate, in percentage points, applied at once and persistent while set. VAT is paid at the new rate at once; shops pass it into their prices over a few months (about 40% in the first month, nearly all within six), keeping the difference in their margins meanwhile. Consumer prices follow, and indexed debts are revalued with them. Setting it back to 0 removes the shift (prices drop back the same way). With the key rate held (locked), a lasting change that keeps unemployment off its normal rate keeps inflation off target: after a lasting tax rise, say, the held rate is too high for the new economy, so prices keep falling while unemployment stays up (Wicksell’s cumulative process). With the key rate held and tax rates fixed, nothing but people’s partial trust in the target anchors prices: expectations are only half anchored to it, so the long-run Phillips curve is not vertical (decisions 0002 §6 and 0014), and the króna follows domestic prices. Output and unemployment keep drifting too, for decades; whether they would ever settle is an open question about the model, not a law of economics (decision 0014). After 20 years with both policy levers locked, income tax +2.5 points leaves output about 3.9% lower (0.6% after a year, 2.1% after five) and unemployment 1.2 points higher, both still moving, with the price level 15% lower and the króna 22% stronger; VAT +2.5 points leaves output 2.1% lower and the price level 6.7% lower, so with the key rate held a VAT rise ends up lowering prices; health spending −3% of GDP leaves output 6% lower and unemployment 3.4 points higher; public investment −3% leaves output 9% lower. Treat such effects beyond a few years as a picture of an economy without its nominal anchor. With the policy levers unlocked, the central bank’s rule, which reads slack from unemployment and slowly learns its neutral rate, brings inflation back: after 20 years within about 0.1 point for VAT and 0.05 for transfers, but benefits +30 points leave unemployment about 1 point higher, and public spending ±3% of GDP leaves inflation up to about 0.3 point (a rise) or 0.7 point (a cut) off target and unemployment 0.2–1.3 points off normal, because public services move jobs more than output and the rule’s estimate of the neutral rate reaches its limit (the lever report shows the rate the economy would need, the implied neutral rate, with the debt rule still reacting to it).

levers.label: Other public services
levers.description: Real change in other public services: administration, police, culture, roads.
levers.definition: Level shift in real spending on other public services, % of baseline GDP a year, persistent while set, split between staff and purchases as at baseline. Setting it back to 0 returns spending to baseline. With the policy levers unlocked, a lasting rise costs output and adds debt in the long run: public services employ many staff for each króna of output, the central bank reads the labour scarcity that brings and holds the key rate higher, and the higher interest bill slows the debt rule. After 20 years at +3% of GDP: health, output 2.5% lower, the key rate 3.9 points and government debt 49 points of GDP higher; education, 3.1% lower, 4.1 points and 50 points; other public services, 1.6% lower, 3.6 points and 47 points; public investment, 0.5% lower, 3.1 points and 43 points. While the central bank measured slack against a fixed capacity, which read slack where there was none, the output losses were about half as large (health 1.2%, education 1.5%) and debt 36–40 points higher (decision 0012). A small open economy would share this adjustment through a stronger real króna, which the model does not yet have, so here it falls on interest rates and debt. A cut mirrors it: output ends higher, with the key rate at zero for long spells. With the key rate held (locked), a lasting change that keeps unemployment off its normal rate keeps inflation off target: after a lasting tax rise, say, the held rate is too high for the new economy, so prices keep falling while unemployment stays up (Wicksell’s cumulative process). With the key rate held and tax rates fixed, nothing but people’s partial trust in the target anchors prices: expectations are only half anchored to it, so the long-run Phillips curve is not vertical (decisions 0002 §6 and 0014), and the króna follows domestic prices. Output and unemployment keep drifting too, for decades; whether they would ever settle is an open question about the model, not a law of economics (decision 0014). After 20 years with both policy levers locked, income tax +2.5 points leaves output about 3.9% lower (0.6% after a year, 2.1% after five) and unemployment 1.2 points higher, both still moving, with the price level 15% lower and the króna 22% stronger; VAT +2.5 points leaves output 2.1% lower and the price level 6.7% lower, so with the key rate held a VAT rise ends up lowering prices; health spending −3% of GDP leaves output 6% lower and unemployment 3.4 points higher; public investment −3% leaves output 9% lower. Treat such effects beyond a few years as a picture of an economy without its nominal anchor. With the policy levers unlocked, the central bank’s rule, which reads slack from unemployment and slowly learns its neutral rate, brings inflation back: after 20 years within about 0.1 point for VAT and 0.05 for transfers, but benefits +30 points leave unemployment about 1 point higher, and public spending ±3% of GDP leaves inflation up to about 0.3 point (a rise) or 0.7 point (a cut) off target and unemployment 0.2–1.3 points off normal, because public services move jobs more than output and the rule’s estimate of the neutral rate reaches its limit (the lever report shows the rate the economy would need, the implied neutral rate, with the debt rule still reacting to it).

levers.label: Who buys new government bonds
levers.description: Banks and the central bank pay with newly created money; pension funds and households pay with existing deposits.
levers.definition: Choice, persistent while set: every new bond sold from then on goes to the chosen buyer, or 40/60 to banks and pension funds in the mix. Pension funds and older households buy only what their deposits can pay for that month; banks take the rest. When the budget is in surplus the government buys bonds back from every holder in proportion to what they hold, whatever the choice. Bonds already sold stay where they are, though pension funds and older households slowly sell surplus bonds to banks to restore their portfolio shares. New bonds pay the key rate plus its spread whoever buys, so the choice changes money and who receives the interest, not interest rates. The central bank earns the bond rate on the bonds it buys and hands its profit to the government, but it pays the key rate on the reserves it creates to buy them, so on those bonds the government saves only the bond rate’s spread over the key rate (0.5 points), not the whole interest bill: with both policy levers locked, after 20 years of 2% of GDP more public investment, the budget balance is about 0.1% of GDP better and debt about 0.7 points of GDP lower than with the mix. Non-residents are not an option: they buy and sell bonds with banks on their own, through the carry trade.

levers.label: Pension funds’ foreign allocation
levers.description: Shifts the target foreign share of pension assets; funds move toward it through new flows, limited by their cash, selling krónur, and the weaker króna revalues what they hold. They also want fewer domestic assets: they lend less of new mortgages, and covered bonds and mortgages cost a little more.
levers.definition: Level shift in the target foreign share, in percentage points of assets, persistent while set. Funds close the gap at up to 0.5 a year, but they buy only with cash above their buffer: new contributions, income, and the bank bonds, deposits and mortgage lending they give up. Shifts of a few points move at about that pace (+5: about 3 points higher after a year and 4 after two). Larger ones are cash-limited for years: at +20 the share is about 8.5–9 points higher after a year, about 10.5 after two and 13.5–15 after five (less with the policy rules acting, where the higher key rate slows the króna’s fall). Part of the rise is the weaker króna raising the value of the foreign assets they already hold: the market prices the krónur the funds sell as they flow, so at +20 the króna is about 16% weaker after fifteen months. While set, the funds want proportionally less of every domestic asset: they lend a smaller share of new mortgages (banks lend the rest), and covered bonds and mortgages carry a funding premium of about 0.15 pp per 5 points. In the first two years the weaker króna lifts inflation, and with it banks’ capital (their indexed loans grow with the CPI), so banks give a small discount on loans that offsets part of the premium: indexed mortgage rates rise about half as much as covered-bond rates at first. Setting it back to 0 makes them sell foreign assets back toward the old share, and the premium goes.
